# Yeasts, moulds and dimorphic fungi

> *Most people carry a yeast in the mouth or gut, and everyone breathes in mould spores every day, yet
> serious fungal disease is uncommon. Most fungi cause disease only when a particular defence fails, so
> where a fungus comes from and which defence holds it in check predict who becomes ill.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Sort the medically important fungi by growth form and by where they come from, and predict from
  these the defence that must fail and who is most at risk.
- Explain how *Candida albicans*, part of the body's own microbiota, causes thrush when the
  microbiota or a local defence changes, and bloodstream infection in hospital patients.
- Relate the three patterns of disease caused by *Aspergillus fumigatus* to the state of the host's
  lungs and neutrophils.
- Explain how *Cryptococcus neoformans* reaches the brain when cell-mediated immunity fails, how its
  capsule protects it on the way, and why the capsule is what the antigen test detects.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main fungus cause disease.
- Tell *C. albicans* from *C. neoformans* by source, capsule, typical disease and the defence whose
  failure matters most.
:::

## The group {#sec-fgrp-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-fgrp-sentence}

The fungi that cause human disease are eukaryotes with a wall of chitin and glucan that live in soil,
on decaying plants or on the body itself, and most of them cause disease only when a particular
defence of the host has failed. Most of the six questions have one answer for the whole group; its
members differ mainly in growth form, in where they come from and in the defence that must fail.

Fungi grow as yeasts or as moulds, and some switch between the two (see [*Fungal
principles*](fungal-principles.qmd)):

- **Yeasts** grow as single round or oval cells that multiply by **budding**: a daughter cell swells
  out from the parent cell, receives a copy of the nucleus and separates.
- **Moulds** grow as **hyphae** (singular hypha), branching, tube-shaped filaments that extend at their
  tips and form a mat, and reproduce by **spores**, small cells made in vast numbers on the hyphae and
  released into the air.
- **Dimorphic fungi** grow as moulds in the environment and as yeasts at body temperature.

| Question | Answer for the medically important fungi |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A eukaryotic cell with a wall of chitin and glucan and ergosterol in its membrane, growing as a yeast, a mould or, in dimorphic fungi, both |
| How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow? | Its own metabolism, absorbing nutrients from its surroundings; the fungi that invade deep tissues grow at body temperature, which most fungi do poorly |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Yeasts bud; moulds extend their hyphae and release spores; resistance to antifungal drugs arises by mutation and selection |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Soil, decaying plants and bird droppings, from which spores or yeasts are inhaled; the body's own microbiota; the keratin of skin, hair and nails, passed on by contact. Most fungal infections are not passed from person to person |
| How does damage happen? | Invasion of tissue when a defence fails, and the inflammation it provokes; allergy to a fungus growing in the airways |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Ergosterol in its membrane and a wall of chitin and glucan: the targets of antifungal drugs |

### Sorting the group {#sec-fgrp-key}

Growth form is visible under the microscope and in culture, so we sort the fungi by it first, and then
by where they come from. Among the moulds are the **dermatophytes**, moulds that live on the keratin
of skin, hair and nails. *Pneumocystis jirovecii* is sorted on its own: it is an
unusual fungus that has no ergosterol and cannot be grown in routine culture.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the medically important fungi by growth form and source]{.tree-title}

- Yeasts
  - From the body's own microbiota: *Candida albicans*
  - From soil contaminated with bird droppings: *Cryptococcus neoformans*
- Moulds
  - From spores in the air: *Aspergillus fumigatus*
  - From infected people, animals or soil, by contact: dermatophytes
- Dimorphic fungi
  - From the environment in South-East Asia: *Talaromyces marneffei*
- An unusual fungus, with no ergosterol, that is not grown in routine culture
  - *P. jirovecii*
:::

Where a fungus comes from predicts where its infection starts and which defence must fail:

| Where it comes from | Where infection starts | Defence that must fail, and who is at risk |
|---|---|---|
| The body's own microbiota | At the mucosa and skin where the fungus lives, or in the blood once a barrier is breached | The resident bacteria and intact mucosa and skin: infants, people given antibacterial drugs or corticosteroids, and hospital patients with a catheter in a large vein |
| Spores in the air | In the lung | Macrophages and neutrophils in the lung: people whose **neutropenia**, an abnormally low neutrophil count, lasts for weeks, as after chemotherapy for leukaemia |
| Soil contaminated with bird droppings, or the environment of a particular region | In the lung, then in the blood and distant organs | **Cell-mediated immunity**, the defence by T cells against infected cells and against organisms that live inside host cells: people with advanced HIV infection |
| Infected people, animals or soil, by contact | In the keratin of the skin, hair and nails | No failure is needed: healthy people are infected |

Work through the key from the growth form, and read at each branch what the trait predicts about the
fungus.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/fungi-key.yml"></div>

## Main organisms {#sec-fgrp-main}

### *Candida albicans*: thrush and bloodstream infection {#sec-fgrp-candida}

*C. albicans* is carried by most healthy people, as a yeast on the lining of the mouth, gut or vagina,
or on the skin. On a surface it grows as budding yeast cells; when it invades the epithelium it forms
filaments. Four defences keep it in check, and most of its diseases follow the loss of one or more of
them:

- The resident bacteria, which occupy the same surfaces and consume the nutrients the yeast would use
  (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-microbiota))
- The intact epithelium of the skin and mucosa
- Cell-mediated immunity, which stops the yeast invading the mucosa
- Neutrophils, which kill yeast cells that reach the tissues or the blood

Most of its infections are **endogenous infections**, caused by an organism the person already
carries, so they follow a change in the host and need no new exposure. **Candidiasis** is infection
with any species of *Candida*, and **thrush** is candidiasis of the lining of the mouth or the vagina.

In hospital, two changes give the yeast a route into the blood. Broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs,
which do not act on fungi, let it multiply in the gut, from which it can cross the gut wall. A
**central venous catheter**, a tube passed through the skin into a large vein, gives it a path from the
skin: the yeast grows along the catheter as a **biofilm**, a community of microbes embedded in a shared
matrix on a surface. **Candidaemia**, *Candida* in the blood, carries the yeast to distant organs.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Oral thrush | With fewer resident bacteria or weaker local defences in the mouth, the yeast multiplies, and its filaments invade the surface of the epithelium, which becomes inflamed | White plaques on the tongue and inside the cheeks of an infant, or of an adult who uses a corticosteroid inhaler for asthma |
| Vaginal candidiasis | Antibacterial drugs reduce the resident bacteria of the vagina, and pregnancy and diabetes favour the yeast; it multiplies and invades the surface of the epithelium | Itching and a thick white discharge a few days after a course of antibacterial drugs |
| Oesophageal candidiasis | When cell-mediated immunity fails, the yeast invades the lining of the oesophagus | Pain on swallowing in advanced HIV infection |
| Bloodstream infection | The yeast crosses the gut wall or enters along a catheter, and the blood carries it to distant organs | Candidaemia in a patient in intensive care, with a fever that continues despite antibacterial drugs; the yeast can settle in the eye and threaten sight, or on the heart valves and cause **infective endocarditis**, infection of the heart valves or the inner lining of the heart |

Three conditions let *C. albicans* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | An infant; a person given antibacterial drugs or a corticosteroid inhaler, or who wears dentures; a woman who is pregnant or has diabetes; a person with advanced HIV infection; a hospital patient with a central venous catheter | Each has lost, or has not yet developed, one of the defences that keep the yeast in check, or offers it more to grow on |
| Where (setting) | The person's own body; for bloodstream infection, the hospital, especially intensive care | Most infections are endogenous: the yeast is already on the mucosa and skin and in the gut |
| How (route) | Overgrowth at the surfaces where it lives; or entry to the blood across the gut wall or along a catheter | Filaments invade the surface of the epithelium; in the blood, yeast cells are carried to the eye and the heart valves |

::: {.callout-important}
## Does *Candida* in a sample mean a *Candida* infection?
A laboratory report that names *Candida* is easily read as a diagnosis. Most people carry
*C. albicans* on their mucosa, however, so it is often grown from samples that pass through the mouth
or come from the vagina, such as sputum coughed up from the lungs or a vaginal swab, in people who have no
candidiasis. Growth from such a sample shows only that the yeast is there, which in most people is
**colonisation**, microbes living and multiplying at a site without causing damage (see [*Microbes
and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-words)).

Candidiasis is shown by signs of disease where the yeast is found, such as white plaques on the
mucosa, or by yeast in a site that is normally sterile, such as the blood.
:::

Step through the two routes *C. albicans* takes: overgrowth where it lives, and entry into the blood.

### *Aspergillus fumigatus*: three patterns, set by the host {#sec-fgrp-aspergillus}

*A. fumigatus* is a mould of soil, compost and decaying plants. It releases spores in such numbers
that they are present in the air everywhere, indoors and outdoors, and everyone breathes them in every
day. Two traits let it reach and grow in the lung: its spores are only a few micrometres across, small
enough to be carried down to the alveoli, and it grows well at body temperature, as most moulds do
not. It is not passed from person to person.

In a healthy lung the spores do no harm. Macrophages in the alveoli engulf and kill them, and
neutrophils attack any spores that germinate into hyphae, which are too large to engulf. What follows
an inhaled spore depends on the state of the lung and of these defences, and gives three patterns of
disease.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Allergy | In a person with asthma, the fungus grows in the mucus of the airways without invading them; the damage comes from the host's allergic response to it, which inflames the airways and plugs them with mucus (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)) | Asthma that becomes harder to control; repeated episodes can damage the airways permanently |
| Fungus ball | The fungus grows inside a cavity left in the lung by earlier disease, such as tuberculosis, and forms a ball of hyphae without invading the lung around it | An **aspergilloma**, a ball of hyphae in an existing cavity in the lung, which can make the person cough up blood |
| Invasive infection | In prolonged neutropenia, hyphae grow through the lung and into the walls of its blood vessels; the vessels clot, the tissue they supply becomes necrotic, and fragments of hyphae carried in the blood reach other organs, including the brain | **Invasive aspergillosis**, infection in which hyphae grow into living tissue, in a patient with leukaemia weeks after chemotherapy |

Three conditions let *A. fumigatus* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | For invasive infection, a person whose neutropenia lasts for weeks, as after chemotherapy for leukaemia or a transplant of blood-forming stem cells; for allergy, a person with asthma; for a fungus ball, a person with a cavity left in the lung by earlier disease | Neutrophils attack hyphae, and without them the hyphae invade; the other two patterns need a lung already altered by disease |
| Where (setting) | The air everywhere, indoors and outdoors, including dust from building work | Spores from soil, compost and decaying plants stay suspended in the air; the mould does not pass from person to person |
| How (route) | Inhaled into the airways and alveoli; in invasive infection, through the walls of blood vessels and on in the blood | The spores are small enough to reach the alveoli, and hyphae that invade vessels are carried in the blood to other organs |

::: {.example}
Building work in a hospital raises dust that carries *A. fumigatus* spores, so patients with
prolonged neutropenia are kept away from it, often in rooms supplied with filtered air.
:::

Step through the two routes *A. fumigatus* takes: into the airways of a person with asthma, and
through the lung of a person with prolonged neutropenia.

### *Cryptococcus neoformans*: the capsule and the brain {#sec-fgrp-cryptococcus}

*C. neoformans* is a yeast that lives in soil contaminated with bird droppings, especially those of
pigeons. It is inhaled in dust and does not pass from person to person. Each yeast cell is surrounded
by a thick **capsule**, a polysaccharide layer outside the cell wall that resists phagocytosis.

In most people, cell-mediated immunity contains the inhaled yeast in the lung, often without
symptoms. The containment depends on **CD4 T cells**, lymphocytes that coordinate the immune response,
including the activity of macrophages and of cytotoxic T cells. When CD4 T cells are lost in advanced HIV infection (see
[*Viruses and the host*](../viruses/virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-cd4)), the yeast multiplies in the lung,
enters the blood and reaches the brain. There it causes **meningitis**, inflammation of the meninges
(the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord), with headache and fever that develop over days
to weeks. It also causes disease in people whose cell-mediated immunity is suppressed by drugs after
an organ transplant.

The capsule is also how the infection is detected. The yeast sheds capsule polysaccharide into the
blood and into the cerebrospinal fluid, which bathes the brain and spinal cord, and an antigen test
detects it there. Under the microscope, cerebrospinal fluid mixed with India ink, which darkens the
background, shows the capsule as a clear halo around each yeast.

::: {.example}
Capsule polysaccharide can be detected in the blood before meningitis develops, so people with
advanced HIV infection can be tested and treated before it begins.
:::

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Infection of the lung | Inhaled yeasts multiply in the alveoli, and in most people cell-mediated immunity contains them | Often no symptoms; sometimes pneumonia |
| Meningitis | When cell-mediated immunity fails, the yeast spreads in the blood to the meninges and brain, where the capsule protects it from phagocytes and it multiplies | Headache and fever that worsen over days to weeks in a person with advanced HIV infection |

Three conditions let *C. neoformans* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A person whose cell-mediated immunity has failed: most often in advanced HIV infection, and also after an organ transplant | CD4 T cells direct the macrophages that contain the yeast in the lung; without them it multiplies and spreads |
| Where (setting) | Soil and dust contaminated with bird droppings, especially of pigeons | The yeast grows in the droppings and is inhaled in dust; it does not pass from person to person |
| How (route) | Inhaled into the alveoli, then carried in the blood to the meninges and brain | The capsule resists phagocytes in the lung and in the blood |

Step through the route *C. neoformans* takes from soil to the brain.

## Beyond the main organisms {#sec-fgrp-beyond}

### Supporting organisms {#sec-fgrp-supporting}

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dermatophytes | The keratin of the skin, hair and nails of people and animals, and soil | Moulds that grow only in keratin, in dead layers of cells, so infection stays at the surface; passed on by contact with infected people, animals or soil | Cause **ringworm** (tinea), infection of the skin, hair or nails by a dermatophyte, named for the ring-shaped, scaly patches it can form on the skin; no worm is involved |
| *P. jirovecii* | The lungs of humans; most people are infected in early childhood without illness | Its membrane contains cholesterol in place of ergosterol, so drugs that act on ergosterol or its synthesis do not work against it; cannot be grown in routine culture | Causes pneumonia in advanced HIV infection and in other failures of cell-mediated immunity, such as during long courses of corticosteroids |
| *T. marneffei* | The environment of South-East Asia and southern China | A dimorphic fungus: a mould in the environment, and small yeast cells inside macrophages at body temperature; probably acquired by inhaling spores | Spreads through the body, with fever and skin lesions, in people with advanced HIV infection, among whom it is common in parts of South-East Asia |

### Later in the course {#sec-fgrp-later}

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *C. albicans* | Obstetrics and gynaecology (vaginal candidiasis); HIV care (oral and oesophageal candidiasis); intensive care (bloodstream infection) |
| *A. fumigatus* | Respiratory medicine (allergy that worsens asthma, and fungus balls); haematology and oncology (invasive infection in prolonged neutropenia) |
| *C. neoformans* | Neurology and HIV care (meningitis) |
| Dermatophytes | Dermatology (ringworm of the skin, hair and nails) |
| *P. jirovecii* | Respiratory medicine and HIV care (pneumonia) |
| *T. marneffei* | HIV care in South-East Asia (infection that spreads through the body) |
